subjective.question: Define mechanics. Into which two branches is it divided?
subjective.answer: Mechanics is a branch of physical sciences which studies the action of force on bodies. Under the action of these forces, bodies are in a state of rest or of motion relative to some frame of reference. Mechanics is further divided into two areas: (i) Statics and (ii) Dynamics. Statics is that branch of mechanics which deals with forces acting on a body which is at rest. Dynamics is that branch of mechanics which deals with accelerated motion.

subjective.question: Define inertial and non-inertial frames of reference.
subjective.answer: An inertial frame of reference is a frame of reference in which the law of inertia and other physics laws are valid. Any frame moving at a constant velocity relative to another frame is also an inertial frame of reference. A non-inertial frame of reference is a reference frame in which the law of inertia does not hold.

subjective.question: Define scalar and vector quantities.
subjective.answer: Distinguish between speed and velocity. A scalar quantity has magnitude only, while a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Speed is a scalar quantity: it is the magnitude of velocity. Velocity is a vector quantity: it has magnitude as well as direction. For example, a body moving at 2 m/s has speed 2 m/s, whereas a body moving with velocity (2i+3j) m/s has both magnitude and direction. Acceleration is a vector quantity.

subjective.question: State the parallelogram law of forces.
subjective.answer: If two forces acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram, then their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing through that point. If the forces P and Q act at an angle theta, the magnitude of the resultant is R = sqrt(P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ cos theta), and its direction is given by tan phi = Q sin theta / (P + Q cos theta), where phi is the angle made by the resultant with force P.

subjective.question: Two forces of magnitude 8 N and 10 N are acting on a particle. Find the resultant of these forces by applying the parallelogram law. Find also the angle made by the resultant with the 10 N force.
subjective.answer: In the force triangle, the angle opposite the resultant is 140 degrees. By the law of cosines, R^2 = 8^2 + 10^2 - 2(8)(10)cos(140 degrees) = 64 + 100 - 160(-0.766) = 286.57, so R = 17 N (approximately). By the law of sines, R/sin(140 degrees) = 8/sin(theta), so sin(theta) = 8 sin(140 degrees)/17 = 0.30, giving theta = 17.6 degrees. Hence the resultant is 17 N, making an angle of 17.6 degrees with the 10 N force.

subjective.question: Two forces of magnitude 10 N and 15 N are the resolved parts of a force of magnitude F N. Find the magnitude of the force F.
subjective.answer: In the force triangle, by the law of sines, 15/sin(30 degrees) = 10/sin(alpha), so sin(alpha) = (10/15) sin(30 degrees) = 1/3, giving alpha = 19.5 degrees. The third angle of the triangle is 180 degrees - 30 degrees - 19.5 degrees = 130.5 degrees. Again by the law of sines, F/sin(130.5 degrees) = 15/sin(30 degrees), so F = 30 sin(130.5 degrees) = 22.8 N.

subjective.question: Resolve a force of 1000 N acting at 40 degrees to the horizontal into its horizontal and vertical components.
subjective.answer: Let Fx and Fy be the horizontal and vertical components of the force. Then Fx = 1000 cos(40 degrees) = 1000 x 0.766 = 766 N, and Fy = 1000 sin(40 degrees) = 1000 x 0.643 = 643 N. Thus the horizontal component is 766 N and the vertical component is 643 N.

subjective.question: In a force triangle, a force of 1000 N is opposite an angle of 60 degrees. Find the force opposite an angle of 70 degrees.
subjective.answer: By the law of sines, Fy/sin(70 degrees) = 1000/sin(60 degrees). Hence Fy = 1000 sin(70 degrees)/sin(60 degrees) = 1000 x 0.9397/0.8660 = 1085 N.

subjective.question: How is the resultant of a system of concurrent coplanar forces found?
subjective.answer: Let Fx and Fy be the sums of the horizontal and vertical components of all the forces. The components of the resultant are Rx = Fx1 + Fx2 + Fx3 + ... + FxN and Ry = Fy1 + Fy2 + Fy3 + ... + FyN. The magnitude of the resultant is R = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2) and its direction is given by theta = tan^-1(Ry/Rx), where theta is the angle made by the resultant with the positive x-axis.

subjective.question: The rectangular components of a resultant force are Rx = 5.51 N and Ry = 10.24 N. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
subjective.answer: The magnitude is R = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2) = sqrt((5.51)^2 + (10.24)^2) = sqrt(30.36 + 104.86) = sqrt(135.22) = 11.63 N. The direction is theta = tan^-1(Ry/Rx) = tan^-1(10.24/5.51) = tan^-1(1.858) = 61.7 degrees with the positive x-axis.

subjective.question: What is meant by equilibrium in one dimension?
subjective.answer: Explain with the example of two weights hung by strings. In equilibrium in one dimension, two weights are hung and supported by strings. On the lower block the two forces balance: T2 = m2 g. On the upper block there are three forces: T1 = m1 g + T2, so T1 = (m1 + m2) g. The upper string has more tension than the lower string. A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all the forces acting on it is zero, i.e. the sum of horizontal forces is zero and the sum of vertical forces is zero.

subjective.question: State and explain Newton's third law of motion.
subjective.answer: Newton's first two laws of motion explain how the motion of a single object changes. Newton's third law describes something else that happens when one object exerts a force on another object. According to Newton's third law of motion, forces always act in equal and opposite pairs: if one body exerts a force on a second body, the second body exerts a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction on the first body. These two forces are called the action and the reaction.

subjective.question: State Lamy's theorem.
subjective.answer: If three coplanar concurrent forces acting at a point are in equilibrium, then each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. That is, if forces P, Q and R are in equilibrium and alpha, beta and gamma are the angles opposite them, then P/sin(alpha) = Q/sin(beta) = R/sin(gamma). Lamy's theorem applies to three coplanar concurrent forces, and the sum of the three angles used must be 360 degrees.

subjective.question: Three concurrent coplanar forces of magnitudes 3 N, 2 N and P N are in equilibrium. Find the angle x which the 2 N force makes with the horizontal, and the value of P.
subjective.answer: Let alpha, beta and gamma be the angles between the forces. From the diagram, gamma = 60 degrees + 90 degrees = 150 degrees. By Lamy's theorem, P/sin(alpha) = 3/sin(beta) = 2/sin(150 degrees). Hence 3/sin(beta) = 2/0.5, so sin(beta) = 0.75. Since beta is obtuse, beta = 180 degrees - 48.6 degrees = 131.4 degrees. The angle x is x = beta - 90 degrees = 41.4 degrees. Since alpha + beta + gamma = 360 degrees, alpha = 360 degrees - 131.4 degrees - 150 degrees = 78.6 degrees. Then P/sin(78.6 degrees) = 2/sin(150 degrees), so P = 4 sin(78.6 degrees) = 3.92 N.

subjective.question: State the (lambda, mu) theorem.
subjective.answer: If two concurrent forces are represented by lambda OA and mu OB, their resultant is given by (lambda + mu) OC, where C divides AB so that AC : CB = mu : lambda. For the (lambda, mu) theorem to be satisfied, the forces should be coplanar. If lambda is negative, the division is external and B lies between A and C.

subjective.question: Two concurrent forces are represented by lambda OA and mu OB. Given OA = i + 3j + 5k and OC = 4i - j + k, where C divides AB so that AC : CB = 2 : 3, find the magnitude of the resultant force.
subjective.answer: Since AC : CB = mu : lambda = 2 : 3, we have lambda = 3 and mu = 2. By the (lambda, mu) theorem, the resultant is R = (lambda + mu) OC = (3 + 2)(4i - j + k) = 5(4i - j + k) = 20i - 5j + 5k. Its magnitude is R = sqrt(20^2 + (-5)^2 + 5^2) = sqrt(400 + 25 + 25) = sqrt(450) = 15 sqrt(2) N (approximately 21.2 N).

subjective.question: Two light strings are attached to a block of mass 20 kg. The block is in equilibrium on a smooth horizontal surface AB with its strings taut. The strings make angles of 60 degrees and 30 degrees with the horizontal on either side of the block, and the tensions in the strings are T N and 75 N respectively. Find the value of T and the magnitude of the contact force acting on the block.
subjective.answer: Resolving horizontally, T cos(60 degrees) = 75 cos(30 degrees), so T = 75 cos(30 degrees)/cos(60 degrees) = 75 x 0.866/0.5 = 130 N. Resolving vertically, the contact force N satisfies N + T sin(60 degrees) + 75 sin(30 degrees) = mg = 20 x 10 = 200 N. Hence N = 200 - 130 sin(60 degrees) - 75 sin(30 degrees) = 200 - 112.5 - 37.5 = 50 N. So the tension T is 130 N and the contact force is 50 N.

subjective.question: What is the triangle law of forces? How are the laws of sines and cosines used to find resultants?
subjective.answer: The triangle law states that if two forces acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by two sides of a triangle taken in order, their resultant is represented by the third side taken in the opposite order. The laws of sines and cosines are used with the force triangle to find the magnitude and direction of the resultant. For example, in the parallelogram-law example, the law of cosines gives R^2 = 8^2 + 10^2 - 2(8)(10)cos(140 degrees) = 286.57, so R = 17 N, and the law of sines gives sin(theta) = 8 sin(140 degrees)/17 = 0.30, so theta = 17.6 degrees. The law of sines and the law of cosines are applicable on any triangle, while trigonometric ratios are applicable on right-angled triangles only.

subjective.question: State the conditions for the equilibrium of a particle under the action of coplanar forces.
subjective.answer: A particle is in equilibrium under the action of coplanar forces when the resultant of all the forces is zero. The conditions are: the sum of the horizontal forces is zero (sum Fx = 0) and the sum of the vertical forces is zero (sum Fy = 0). Equivalently, the sum of the rightward forces equals the sum of the leftward forces, and the sum of the upward forces equals the sum of the downward forces. If a body is in vertical equilibrium only, then sum Fy = 0 but sum Fx is not zero; if a horizontal force is removed, the particle remains in vertical equilibrium only.

subjective.question: A body of weight 5 N hangs in equilibrium by a light inextensible string. Find the tension in the string. What happens to the tension if the mass of the body is doubled?
subjective.answer: Since the body is in equilibrium, the tension in the string balances the weight of the body, so the tension is 5 N. The tension equals the weight: T = mg. If the mass of the body is doubled, the weight is doubled, so the tension is also doubled, becoming 10 N. In general, halving the weight halves the tension, and trebling the upward forces requires the downward forces to be trebled to keep the body in equilibrium.
